objectives: Declare a terraform block with required_providers pinning hashicorp/aws to ~> 5.0 and an aws provider block with region = "us-east-1"; do NOT declare a backend block since backend config is managed externally.

Create a data "aws_iam_policy_document" (or aws_iam_role assume-role policy data source) defining the trust policy for Service Catalog, with a sts:AssumeRole action whose Principal is the service principal servicecatalog.amazonaws.com, and scope the trust with a sts:ExternalId condition if an external id is used.

Create resource "aws_iam_role" "test_role" (name = "test_role") using the Service-Catalog assume-role policy document above, so the role can be attached as a launch constraint to a Service Catalog product/portfolio.

Create a scoped launch-constraint IAM policy as a resource "aws_iam_policy" (or aws_iam_role_policy) granting only the actions the provisioned products need — e.g. cloudformation:CreateStack/DescribeStacks/DeleteStack, s3:GetObject/PutObject, and iam:PassRole — with Resources restricted to the specific role ARN (aws_iam_role.test_role.arn) and any bucket ARNs created in this configuration; never pair Action = "*" with Resource = "*" in the same statement.
Attach the launch-constraint policy to test_role with resource "aws_iam_role_policy_attachment" (never aws_iam_policy_attachment, which is destructive).

Create resource "aws_iam_group" for the governance/console group, and attach a scoped group policy that allows members to sts:AssumeRole only the test_role ARN (aws_iam_role.test_role.arn), using aws_iam_group_policy or aws_iam_policy + aws_iam_group_policy_attachment.

Create resource "aws_iam_user" for the console-enabled governance user, and enable console login with resource "aws_iam_user_login_profile" — the password must come from a resource "random_password" value (marked sensitive, never a plaintext literal or variable default in the configuration).
Add the console user to the governance group with resource "aws_iam_group_membership" referencing aws_iam_user.<user>.name and aws_iam_group.<group>.name, so group-level policy inheritance applies.
Do NOT use deprecated aws_iam_policy_attachment, do NOT define aws_s3_bucket_acl, and do NOT mix count and for_each on any IAM resource in this configuration.

Never hardcode AWS account IDs, ARNs, or resource IDs — derive the account via data "aws_caller_identity" "current" and build any needed ARNs from aws_iam_role.test_role.arn / aws_iam_group.<group>.arn / aws_iam_user.<user>.arn or with format() against data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id.

Use snake_case resource labels, keep every resource type+label pair unique, and use only Terraform references (e.g. aws_iam_role.test_role.arn) instead of literal values where a resource attribute is available.

Define a variables/locals block (with defaults) only for non-infrastructure values such as environment name and tag map (e.g. Project, Environment, ManagedBy = "terraform"), and apply those tags consistently to every taggable IAM resource.

Expose outputs for integration with Service Catalog and downstream testing: role name, role ARN (aws_iam_role.test_role.arn), group name, user name, user ARN, and the generated console password marked sensitive = true so `terraform apply` can run unattended without leaking secrets to logs.

Ensure the configuration is fully self-contained for the greenfield account: no data sources that look up pre-existing VPCs, subnets, security groups, key pairs, S3 buckets, secrets, or SSM parameters, and no hardcoded ami-*, vpc-*, subnet-*, sg-*, or externally-owned ARN values.

remediation_history.formatted_errors:
### TERRAFORM STRUCTURAL Errors
**terraform-validate (provider schema):**
  - [ERROR] | line 286 | Value for unconfigurable attribute | Can't configure a value for "password": its value will be decided automatically based on the result of applying this configuration.
remediation_history.suggestion:
### Root Cause Analysis

- **Single error, single root cause.** The only structural failure is `terraform-validate` rejecting `password` on `aws_iam_user_login_profile.governance` (line 286). The AWS provider marks this attribute as **computed-only**: the login-profile password is generated automatically at apply time and cannot be supplied from configuration.
- **No Checkov/Trivy errors are present in this iteration**, so there is nothing to consolidate — but the fix must not reintroduce a plaintext secret to satisfy the original "password from `random_password`" objective. Those two goals are mutually exclusive with this resource type: the provider does not accept a user-supplied password.
- **Downstream consequence of the fix:** once `password` is removed, `random_password.console_password` (and its output reference) has no consumer, and the `console_password` output must instead source the provider-generated value.

### Fix Objectives

1. **Remove the `password` argument from `resource "aws_iam_user_login_profile" "governance"`.** This is the direct cause of the "Value for unconfigurable attribute" error. The attribute is computed-only; the provider generates the password internally on create. Keep `user`, `password_reset_required`, and optionally `password_length` only.

2. **Repoint the `console_password` output to the resource's computed attribute** — i.e. reference `aws_iam_user_login_profile.governance.password` (this attribute is only populated when `pgp_key` is not set, which is the case here). Keep `sensitive = true` so `terraform apply` stays unattended and never writes the secret to the plan/log. Optionally set `password_reset_required = false` for test usability, or leave `true` and document that the emitted value is a first-login temporary credential — either choice avoids re-declaring a configurable password.

3. **Remove the now-orphaned `resource "random_password" "console_password"`** (and its output reference). Since the login-profile password cannot be set from Terraform, this resource has no valid consumer; leaving it in place is dead configuration that will mislead future iterations and can trigger unused-resource lint findings. If a deterministic, retrievable secret is genuinely required later, the correct provider-native mechanism is `pgp_key` on the login profile with an `encrypted_password` output — not a `password` argument — but that is a separate feature, not part of this fix.

4. **Leave the `random` provider declaration in `required_providers` untouched for now** (it is harmless and unused) — do not add or remove providers as part of this change; only the resource and output references above are affected.

5. **Re-run `terraform validate` after the edit** to confirm the sole remaining error class (unconfigurable attribute) is cleared and that no new reference error is introduced by the output rewiring; confirm Checkov/Trivy surface no new findings for the rebuilt login profile.

flat_errors: [AWS-0132] HIGH: S3 encryption should use Customer Managed Keys — Bucket does not encrypt data with a customer managed key.
remediation_history.formatted_errors:
### TRIVY Errors
  - [AWS-0132] HIGH: S3 encryption should use Customer Managed Keys — Bucket does not encrypt data with a customer managed key.
remediation_history.suggestion:
### Root Cause Analysis

- **Single finding, single root cause.** Iteration 1's `terraform validate` error is resolved (the `password` argument is gone). The only outstanding issue is a **Trivy AWS-0132 (HIGH)** finding: the artifacts bucket's default encryption uses `sse_algorithm = "AES256"` (SSE-S3 / AWS-managed keys), which the policy treats as "no customer managed key." The Rego rule fails when `bucket.encryption.kmskeyid` is empty — so the fix is to introduce a real CMK and point `kms_master_key_id` at it.
- **No Checkov errors and no structural errors are present**, so nothing to consolidate. The fix is additive: one new KMS resource plus an edit to the existing encryption configuration.
- **Downstream correctness consequence (not a validator error, but must be handled):** once objects are encrypted with SSE-KMS, the `test_role` launch-constraint role needs `kms:Decrypt` / `kms:GenerateDataKey` / `kms:DescribeKey` on that key, otherwise its `s3:GetObject` / `s3:PutObject` grants will fail at runtime. This is part of the same logical fix even though only the encryption line is flagged.

### Fix Objectives

1. **Create a customer managed key for the artifacts bucket** as a new `resource "aws_kms_key"` block (e.g. label `artifacts`). This is the object the encryption config will reference; do not introduce any hardcoded key ARNs or account IDs.

2. **Apply KMS hardening attributes on the key**: `description` referencing the artifacts bucket, `deletion_window_in_days` (e.g. 7 for a test stack), and `enable_key_rotation = true`. Add `tags = local.common_tags` so the key participates in the stack's tagging convention. This satisfies the CMK intent and is the expected best-practice companion to the AWS-0132 fix rather than a suppression.

3. **Optionally add an `aws_kms_alias`** (e.g. `alias/<project>-<environment>-artifacts`) pointing at the key ARN, so downstream Service Catalog/test tooling can reference a stable, human-readable name. This is optional but recommended; it must use `aws_kms_key.artifacts.arn`, never a literal.

4. **Update the existing `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration.artifacts` rule** so `apply_server_side_encryption_by_default` sets `sse_algorithm = "aws:kms"` and `kms_master_key_id = aws_kms_key.artifacts.arn`. This is the direct fix for the AWS-0132 finding — it converts the "empty kmskeyid" state into a CMK-backed state.

5. **Add `bucket_key_enabled = true`** to that same SSE rule block. It keeps the CMK requirement satisfied while reducing KMS API call cost/volume for S3 traffic (S3 Bucket Keys), which is the recommended pairing for SSE-KMS on a data bucket.

6. **Extend the `data.aws_iam_policy_document.launch_constraint` policy document with a KMS statement** granting the launch-constraint role the operations it now needs against the CMK: `kms:Decrypt`, `kms:GenerateDataKey`, and `kms:DescribeKey`. Scope `resources` to `aws_kms_key.artifacts.arn` only (no `"*"` resource, no wildcard action pairing). Without this the role cannot read/write the now-KMS-encrypted objects it was already granted `s3:*Object` access to.

7. **Do not add a restrictive inline KMS key policy that blocks the role/account.** The default key policy grants the account root full use of the key, which is sufficient for the S3 service to encrypt/decrypt on behalf of the role. If a key policy statement is added for defense-in-depth, derive the principal with `data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id` (or build the root ARN via `format("arn:%s:iam::%s:root", data.aws_partition.current.partition, data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id)`) — never a hardcoded account number.

8. **Add an output for the CMK** (e.g. `kms_key_arn` = `aws_kms_key.artifacts.arn`, plus optionally the alias) so Service Catalog product/portfolio configuration and downstream tests can reference the key. Follow the existing output style; do not mark it sensitive.

9. **Re-run Terraform validate, Checkov, and Trivy** after the change to confirm AWS-0132 clears, the validate stage stays clean, and no new finding (e.g. KMS key rotation, key deletion window) is introduced by the added resources.
remediation_history.retriever_context:
### [AVD-AWS-0132] S3 encryption should use Customer Managed Keys (Severity: HIGH)
Description: Encryption using AWS keys provides protection for your S3 buckets. To gain greater control over encryption, such as key rotation, access policies, and auditability, use customer managed keys (CMKs) with SSE-KMS.
Note that SSE-KMS is not supported for S3 server access logging destination buckets; in such cases, use SSE-S3 instead.
Remediation (Terraform): Use SSE-KMS with a customer managed key (CMK)
Terraform Good Example:
```hcl
resource "aws_kms_key" "mykey" {}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "good_example" {
  bucket = "mybucket"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration" "example" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.good_example.id

  rule {
    apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
      kms_master_key_id = aws_kms_key.mykey.arn
      sse_algorithm     = "aws:kms"
    }
  }
}
```
Policy (Rego):
```rego
package builtin.aws.s3.aws0132

import rego.v1

import data.lib.cloud.value

deny contains res if {
	some bucket in input.aws.s3.buckets

	# Log buckets don't support non AES256 encryption - this rule doesn't apply here
	# https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/s3-server-access-log-not-delivered/
	not log_bucket(bucket)

	without_cmk(bucket)

	res := result.new(
		"Bucket does not encrypt data with a customer managed key.",
		object.get(bucket, "encryption", bucket),
	)
}

# The LogDelivery group gets WRITE and READ_ACP permissions on the bucket
log_bucket(bucket) if lower(bucket.acl.value) == "log-delivery-write"

# https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/enable-server-access-logging.html#grant-log-delivery-permissions-acl
log_bucket(bucket) if {
	some grant in bucket.grants
	grant.grantee.uri.value == "http://acs.amazonaws.com/groups/s3/LogDelivery"
	some permission in grant.permissions
	permission.value in {"WRITE", "FULL_CONTROL"}
}

# https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/enable-server-access-logging.html#grant-log-delivery-permissions-bucket-policy
log_bucket(bucket) if {
	some policy in bucket.bucketpolicies
	doc := json.unmarshal(policy.document.value)
	some statement in doc.Statement
	lower(statement.Effect) == "allow"
	"logging.s3.amazonaws.com" in statement.Principal.Service
	some action in statement.Action
	lower(action) == "s3:putobject"
}

without_cmk(bucket) if value.is_empty(bucket.encryption.kmskeyid)

without_cmk(bucket) if not bucket.encryption.kmskeyid
```
